questions.question: How many straight chain esters have the formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$?
questions.answer: The ester $\text{R-COO-R}'$ has 6 carbons in total, so the carbons in the acid-derived part and the alcohol-derived part must add to 6 (with 1 to 5 carbons in the acid part). The straight chain esters are: methyl pentanoate, ethyl butanoate, propyl propanoate, butyl ethanoate and pentyl methanoate. That is 5 esters.

questions.question:
The chart below shows the colour ranges for three common indicators: methyl orange (red below about pH 3, yellow above about pH 4.5); bromothymol blue (yellow below about pH 6, blue above about pH 7.5); phenolphthalein (colourless below about pH 8.3, pink above about pH 10).

Equal volumes of a particular solution are poured into three separate beakers and a few drops of one indicator only is added to each beaker. The resulting colours are shown below.

| Indicator | Colour |
|---|---|
| Bromothymol blue | Yellow |
| Methyl orange | Yellow |
| Phenolphthalein | Colourless |

What is the pH range of the solution?
questions.answer: Methyl orange is yellow only above pH $\approx4.5$, so pH $>4.5$. Bromothymol blue is yellow only below pH $\approx6.0$, so pH $<6.0$. Phenolphthalein is colourless below pH 8.3, which is consistent with this. Together the pH range is 4.5 – 6.0.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about equilibrium systems is true?
questions.answer: The endothermic direction has the higher activation energy, so raising the temperature increases the number of collisions with energy of at least the activation energy by a greater amount in the endothermic direction than in the exothermic direction. This is why the position of equilibrium shifts towards the endothermic direction, so A is true. Pressure has no link to which direction is endothermic (B). Increasing the volume decreases the collision frequency on both sides, and the side with more gas particles is affected more by a pressure change, not 'increased' by a volume increase (C). Increasing concentration is not tied to the number of moles of gas (D).
options: Increasing the temperature of an equilibrium system causes a greater increase in the number of collisions in the endothermic direction than in the exothermic direction.
Increasing the pressure of an equilibrium system causes a greater increase in the number of collisions in the endothermic direction than in the exothermic direction.
Increasing the volume of an equilibrium system causes a greater increase in the number of collisions in the side with more moles of gas than the side with fewer moles of gas.
Increasing the concentration of an equilibrium system causes a greater increase in the number of collisions in the side with more moles of gas than the side with the fewer moles of gas.

questions.question:
Nylon 6,6 is a polymer with the following structure: $-\text{C(=O)-(CH}_2)_4\text{-C(=O)-NH-(CH}_2)_6\text{-NH-C(=O)-(CH}_2)_4\text{-C(=O)-NH-(CH}_2)_6\text{-NH}-$. Which combination gives the correct monomers used and the type of polymerisation undergone to form nylon 6,6?

| | Monomer | Monomer | Type of polymerisation |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | $\text{HOOC(CH}_2)_4\text{COOH}$ | $\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2)_6\text{NH}_2$ | addition |
| B | $\text{HOOC(CH}_2)_4\text{COOH}$ | $\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2)_6\text{NH}_2$ | condensation |
| C | $\text{HOOC(CH}_2)_4\text{NH}_2$ | $\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2)_6\text{COOH}$ | addition |
| D | $\text{HOOC(CH}_2)_4\text{NH}_2$ | $\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2)_6\text{COOH}$ | condensation |
questions.answer: Cutting each amide link ($-\text{CO-NH}-$) gives a dicarboxylic acid with 4 $\text{CH}_2$ groups, hexanedioic acid $\text{HOOC(CH}_2)_4\text{COOH}$, and a diamine with 6 $\text{CH}_2$ groups, 1,6-diaminohexane $\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2)_6\text{NH}_2$. Each amide bond forms with the loss of a water molecule, so this is condensation polymerisation.

questions.question: A sample liquid of compound Q did not decolourise acidified potassium permanganate when it was added to it. Which of the following is a possible identity for compound Q?
questions.answer: Acidified permanganate is decolourised by alkenes (C=C) and by primary and secondary alcohols (which are oxidised). Pentan-1-ol is primary, pentan-2-ol is secondary and cyclopentene is an alkene, so all would decolourise it. 2-Methylpentan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol and cannot be oxidised, so the purple colour remains.

questions.question: The diagram shows the components of an atomic absorption spectrophotometer (hollow cathode lamp, flame fed by a nebuliser from the test solution, monochromator, detector and data processor). Which component allows for a valid experiment to be carried out when testing for the concentration of a particular metal ion in a solution that contains other metal ions?
questions.answer: The hollow cathode lamp contains the metal being analysed, so it emits light at the specific wavelengths that only atoms of that metal absorb. Other metal ions in the sample do not absorb these wavelengths, so the absorbance depends only on the concentration of the target metal. The flame atomises the sample, the monochromator isolates a wavelength and the detector measures intensity, but none of them provides the selectivity for a particular metal.

questions.question: Bitter yams contain high levels of toxic oxalates. In the Tiwi Islands, bitter yam plants are placed in streams for several days as part of a ritual to make the plants safe to eat. Which concept does this best demonstrate?
questions.answer: The yam is placed in flowing water, so the dissolved oxalate is carried away and fresh water continually replaces it. Matter is exchanged with the surroundings, so this is an open system. The oxalates dissolve out without ever reaching equilibrium because the stream removes them.

questions.question: What is the name of the compound drawn?
questions.answer: The longest chain runs from the $\text{H}_3\text{C}$ end through the carbon carrying the ethyl group and on to the carbon bonded to bromine and the terminal $\text{CH}_3$: 7 carbons (heptane). Numbering from the bromine end gives Br on C2 and the ethyl group on C4, so the name is 2-bromo-4-ethylheptane. Prefixes are in alphabetical order (bromo before ethyl), which rules out C.

questions.question: The mass of magnesium carbonate that will dissolve in 1 L of water is closest to
questions.answer: Using $K_{sp}(\text{MgCO}_3)=6.8\times10^{-6}$ (data sheet): $\text{MgCO}_3(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq)+\text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq)$, so $s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}=\sqrt{6.8\times10^{-6}}=2.6\times10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$. $m=2.6\times10^{-3}\times84.31=0.22$ g.

questions.question:
The mass spectrum for a position isomer of propanol is shown (base peak at $m/z=31$, with smaller peaks at 15, 29, 43, 45 and a molecular ion at 60). Which isomer of propanol was analysed and what fragment could confirm this?

| | Isomer | Fragment ($m/z$) |
|---|---|---|
| A | Propan-1-ol | 43 |
| B | Propan-1-ol | 29 |
| C | Propan-2-ol | 31 |
| D | Propan-2-ol | 45 |
questions.answer: The base peak at $m/z=31$ is $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}^+$, formed by cleavage next to the OH-bearing carbon of a primary alcohol, so the compound is propan-1-ol. Propan-2-ol would instead have a base peak at 45, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHOH}^+$, so C and D are wrong. The peak at 29, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5^+$, is also present in propan-1-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ loses $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), while 43 ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^+$) is not a fragment that confirms an isomer. Of the options given, B (propan-1-ol with the 29 fragment) is the correct pair.

questions.question: A solution contained a mixture of ions comprised of magnesium, calcium and lead. Which of the following correctly lists the reagents in an order whereby the metals could be individually isolated via selective precipitation?
questions.answer: Adding NaCl first precipitates only lead as $\text{PbCl}_2$ (calcium and magnesium chlorides are soluble). After filtering, $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$ precipitates calcium as $\text{CaSO}_4$ (magnesium sulfate is soluble). Finally $\text{Na}_3\text{PO}_4$ precipitates magnesium as $\text{Mg}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$. In A, carbonate would precipitate all three metals together, and in C and D the first reagent is either a formula that does not exist (NaSO$_4$, NaCO$_3$) or precipitates nothing (nitrates are all soluble).

questions.question: When pure ammonium chloride is dissolved in pure water at $25^\circ$C, the pH of the final solution is less than 7. Which statement best explains why the pH $<7$ for the resultant solution?
questions.answer: $\text{NH}_4^+$ is the conjugate acid of the weak base $\text{NH}_3$, so it donates protons to water: $\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{NH}_3(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$. The hydronium ions formed make the solution acidic. $\text{Cl}^-$ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and does not affect pH.
options: Ammonium ions accept protons from water, leaving hydroxide ions in solution.
Chloride ions make the solution acidic.
Ammonium ions combine with water molecules to give ammonium hydroxide.
Water molecules accept protons from ammonium ions forming hydronium ions in solution.

questions.question: The carbon-13 NMR spectrum for butan-2-amine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(NH}_2)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, is shown (four signals, at 10.4, 23.8, 33.0 and 48.6 ppm). Which signal corresponds to the carbon atom directly attached to the amine group?
questions.answer: The electronegative nitrogen deshields the carbon it is bonded to, shifting its signal furthest downfield. The most downfield signal, 48.6 ppm, is therefore the $\text{CH}$ carbon bonded to $\text{NH}_2$.

questions.question: Iodine, a silver solid, sublimes to produce a purple gas. A crystal of iodine was placed into a sealed container. When equilibrium was reached at $t=20$ minutes, a purple gas could be seen. A change was made to the system and a new equilibrium was established which had a more intense purple colour to the gas, compared to the colour at $t=20$ minutes. Which change could account for a more intense purple colour, as outlined above?
questions.answer: The equilibrium is $\text{I}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{I}_2(g)$ with $K=[\text{I}_2(g)]$, which depends only on temperature. Sublimation is endothermic, so raising the temperature increases $K$ and the concentration of purple $\text{I}_2(g)$ at the new equilibrium. Changing the volume or pressure, or adding more solid, does not change $[\text{I}_2(g)]$ at the new equilibrium.
options: The pressure of the system was reduced.
The volume of the container was halved.
The temperature of the container was increased.
More crystal was added to the container.

questions.question: The molar heat of neutralisation is $-55$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. What is the heat released when 40 mL of $0.40$ mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide reacts with 100 mL of $0.10$ mol L$^{-1}$ sulfuric acid?
questions.answer: $n(\text{OH}^-)=0.040\times0.40=0.016$ mol. $n(\text{H}^+)=2\times0.100\times0.10=0.020$ mol. $\text{OH}^-$ is limiting, so 0.016 mol of water forms: heat released $=0.016\times55=0.88$ kJ.

questions.question: An experiment was carried out to synthesise butyl ethanoate. The resultant mixture was transferred to a separating funnel as illustrated in the diagram (a top layer and a bottom layer). Which of the following tests could be used to determine the presence of unreacted carboxylic acid molecules?
questions.answer: The ester is less dense than water and is almost insoluble in it, so it forms the top layer. The unreacted ethanoic acid (very soluble in water) is mostly in the aqueous bottom layer. Adding sodium hydrogencarbonate to the bottom layer gives bubbles of $\text{CO}_2$ if a carboxylic acid is present. Sodium metal would react with the water, so B is not a valid test, a fruity smell indicates only the ester, and dichromate does not react with carboxylic acids.
options: Addition of sodium metal to the bottom layer.
Isolating the top layer and checking for a fruity smell.
Reacting the top layer with $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ and a few drops of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.

questions.question: 12 mL of a gaseous hydrocarbon was reacted with 90 mL of oxygen at $25^\circ$C. On cooling to $25^\circ$C, the residual mixture of gases had a volume of 72 mL. This was shaken with potassium hydroxide solution to remove the carbon dioxide and, as a consequence, the volume of gas dropped to 36 mL consisting of oxygen only. What was the gaseous hydrocarbon?
questions.answer: Volume of $\text{CO}_2=72-36=36$ mL, so each hydrocarbon molecule gives $36/12=3$ carbon atoms. Oxygen used $=90-36=54$ mL, which is $54/12=4.5$ per molecule. For $\text{C}_3\text{H}_y$: $3+y/4=4.5$, so $y=6$ and the hydrocarbon is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$, propene. (Propane would need 5 volumes of oxygen.)

questions.question:
A molecule of butane, $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$, is shown with signal $X$ marking the hydrogens of a terminal $\text{CH}_3$ group and signal $Y$ marking the hydrogens of the adjacent $\text{CH}_2$ group. What is the multiplicity of signals $X$ and $Y$ in the $^1$H spectrum of butane?

| | $X$ | $Y$ |
|---|---|---|
| A | Triplet | Quartet |
| B | Quartet | Triplet |
| C | Triplet | Sextet |
| D | Quartet | Quintet |
questions.answer:
By the $n+1$ rule, the terminal $\text{CH}_3$ ($X$) has 2 neighbouring hydrogens on the adjacent $\text{CH}_2$, so it is a triplet. The $\text{CH}_2$ ($Y$) has $3+2=5$ neighbouring hydrogens (the $\text{CH}_3$ and the other $\text{CH}_2$), so it is split into $5+1=6$ lines, a sextet.

Note: the school's paper listed this option as "Triplet / Quintet", which is not correct for butane (a quintet would need 4 neighbouring hydrogens). The option has been corrected to a sextet so that the question has a correct answer.

questions.question: In the fermentation of a glucose ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$) sample, 5.6 L of gas was produced at $35^\circ$C and 95 kPa of pressure. What mass of ethanol was produced in this fermentation reaction?
questions.answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq)\rightarrow2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)+2\text{CO}_2(g)$. The gas is $\text{CO}_2$: $n=\dfrac{PV}{RT}=\dfrac{95\times5.6}{8.314\times308.15}=0.2077$ mol. Ethanol and $\text{CO}_2$ are produced in a 1:1 ratio, so $m(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})=0.2077\times46.07=9.6$ g.

questions.question:
A gaseous reaction between molecules A and B occurs as follows: $\text{A}(g)+\text{B}(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{C}(g)+\text{D}(g)$, $\Delta H=12$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. A and B are introduced into a sealed reaction vessel, and the system comes to equilibrium by $t=0.4$ s. At $t=0.5$ s a change is made to the system and the system re-establishes a new equilibrium. A graph of reaction rate as a function of time is shown (forward and reverse rates are equal before $t=0.5$ s; at $t=0.5$ s both rates increase, the reverse rate rises above the forward rate and then both settle at the same, higher, value). Which of the following changes to the system is consistent with the reaction rate graphs?

| | Change occurring at $t=0.5$ s |
|---|---|
| A | Doubling of reaction volume |
| B | Increase of reaction temperature |
| C | Halving of reaction volume |
| D | Decrease of reaction temperature |
questions.answer: Both rates rise at $t=0.5$ s, so the particles are more concentrated or have more energy. Doubling the volume or lowering the temperature would lower both rates (A, D). Raising the temperature would raise both rates, but because the forward reaction is endothermic the forward rate would increase more, shifting the equilibrium forwards (B). The graph shows the reverse rate jumping above the forward rate. Halving the volume doubles the concentrations of all gases, raising both rates, and the system shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas (2 mol A+B on the left, 3 mol on the right), which is the reverse direction, so the reverse rate is momentarily larger. This is consistent with C.

questions.question:
Discuss the changes in the development of theories of acids and bases with reference to the Arrhenius and Brønsted–Lowry theories using the chemical reaction below.
$$\text{HCl}(g)+\text{NH}_3(g)\rightarrow\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$$
questions.answer:
**Arrhenius theory:** an acid is a substance that produces $\text{H}^+$ ions in aqueous solution and a base is a substance that produces $\text{OH}^-$ ions in aqueous solution, e.g. $\text{HCl}(aq)+\text{NaOH}(aq)\rightarrow\text{NaCl}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. It could not explain bases that do not contain hydroxide (such as ammonia or carbonate) or acid–base reactions that occur without water, such as the reaction above between gaseous $\text{HCl}$ and gaseous $\text{NH}_3$, which has no $\text{H}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$ ions produced in solution.

**Brønsted–Lowry theory:** a broader definition in which an acid is a proton ($\text{H}^+$) donor and a base is a proton acceptor, so an acid–base reaction is a proton transfer. It is not limited to aqueous solutions or to hydroxide-containing bases. In the reaction given, $\text{HCl}$ donates a proton and is the acid, and $\text{NH}_3$ accepts the proton (using its lone pair) and is the base, forming $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$, which together make $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$. The change from the Arrhenius to the Brønsted–Lowry theory therefore extended the model to explain reactions that Arrhenius could not.

questions.question: Ammonia is a weak base with a $K_b$ value of $1.8\times10^{-5}$. Determine the pH of a $0.500$ mol L$^{-1}$ ammonia solution.

The graph shows a titration of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide (pH against volume of base added, with a sharp rise at the equivalence point). State where on the curve the buffering zone is found, and mark with an "X" the point at which the buffer is most effective.
questions.answer: The buffering zone is the gently sloping region of the curve before the equivalence point, where the solution contains both ethanoic acid and its conjugate base (ethanoate). It is most effective at the half-way point to the equivalence point (half the volume of base needed to reach the end point), where $[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}]=[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-]$ and $pH=pK_a$. The "X" belongs at this half-way point, on the flattish part of the curve below the steep rise.

questions.question: For the titration of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide (see the graph above), explain the chemical reactions in the buffering zone.
questions.answer: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid, so in solution there is an equilibrium: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$. As $\text{NaOH}$ is added, the hydroxide ions react with the acid: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ (the added $\text{OH}^-$ also removes $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, shifting the ionisation equilibrium to the right by Le Chatelier's principle). In this region the solution contains a significant amount of both ethanoic acid and its conjugate base, ethanoate, so the added $\text{OH}^-$ is consumed and the pH changes only slightly. This continues until almost all the $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ has been used up (the equivalence point), after which there is nothing to neutralise the added $\text{OH}^-$ and the pH rises sharply.

questions.question:
A diesel engine vehicle can use either petrodiesel or biodiesel as a fuel. Some properties of the two fuels are given below.

| Fuel | Major component | Energy content (MJ kg$^{-1}$) | Density (kg L$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Petrodiesel | $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{26}$ | 43 | 0.89 |
| Biodiesel | $\text{C}_{19}\text{H}_{32}\text{O}_2$ | 38 | 0.89 |

Assume that combustion occurs in an unlimited supply of oxygen and use the data from the table to calculate the number of litres of biodiesel that are required to be burnt to produce the same amount of energy as 2.5 kg of petrodiesel.
questions.answer:
Energy from 2.5 kg petrodiesel $=2.5\times43=107.5$ MJ.

Mass of biodiesel needed $=\dfrac{107.5}{38}=2.83$ kg.

Volume $=\dfrac{m}{\rho}=\dfrac{2.83}{0.89}=3.18$ L.

questions.question: Suggest ONE advantage of using biodiesel instead of petrodiesel.
questions.answer: Biodiesel is made from renewable sources (plant oils and animal fats that can be regrown), whereas petrodiesel is made from fossil fuels, which are non-renewable and finite. (Alternatively, biodiesel contains oxygen in its molecules and so tends to undergo more complete combustion.)

questions.question:
Cinnamaldehyde is an organic molecule responsible for the cinnamon flavour and odour in food products. It is commonly synthesised from benzaldehyde and ethanal using $\text{NaOH}$. The benzaldehyde precursor can be derived from one of two reaction pathways: Pathway 1 converts toluene to dichloromethylbenzene using $\text{Cl}_2$ and heat, and then converts this to benzaldehyde using $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and heat. Pathway 2 converts benzene directly to benzaldehyde using $\text{CO}$ and $\text{HCl}$ with a catalyst.

Discuss the design considerations made for these reaction pathways.
questions.answer:
**Temperature (Pathway 1):** both steps use heat, which increases the kinetic energy of the reactant particles so that more collisions have enough energy to react, increasing the rate and reducing the time required. However, heating adds energy and equipment costs.

**Catalyst (Pathway 2):** the catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so the reaction proceeds at a faster rate and can operate at a lower temperature, reducing energy costs and improving efficiency.

**Number of steps (atom economy):** Pathway 2 makes benzaldehyde in a single step, which gives a higher atom economy, uses fewer materials and produces less waste. Pathway 1 has two steps, and a multistep process loses some yield at every stage, so the overall yield is lower.

**Hazards:** both pathways use hazardous reagents ($\text{Cl}_2$ in Pathway 1; toxic $\text{CO}$ and corrosive $\text{HCl}$ in Pathway 2), so safe handling procedures (fume cupboards, ventilation, gas monitoring) must be considered in the design.

questions.question:
The endpoint of a titration may be determined using a conductivity meter. The conductivity was measured as 0.01 mol L$^{-1}$ potassium hydroxide was added to 10.00 mL of hydrochloric acid, as shown.

| KOH added (mL) | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conductivity (S m$^{-1}$) | 130 | 116 | 103 | 89 | 76 | 73 | 87 | 103 |

Describe how the conductivity changes during the titration and explain this using the ions present. Use two lines of best fit through the data to determine the volume of KOH at the endpoint.
questions.answer:
When the data are plotted (conductivity against volume of KOH added) the points fall on two straight lines that intersect at a minimum.

Before the endpoint the conductivity falls steadily (about $-13.5$ S m$^{-1}$ per mL). Highly mobile $\text{H}^+$ ions are removed by the added $\text{OH}^-$ (forming water) and replaced by less mobile $\text{K}^+$ ions, so the conductivity decreases.

After the endpoint the conductivity rises steadily (about $+15$ S m$^{-1}$ per mL) because excess $\text{K}^+$ and highly mobile $\text{OH}^-$ ions accumulate in the solution.

The two best-fit lines intersect at about $4.6$ mL, which is the volume of KOH at the endpoint (the minimum conductivity, about $67$ S m$^{-1}$ at the intersection).

questions.question: In the titration of hydrochloric acid with potassium hydroxide monitored by conductivity (see the data above), account for the conductivity value not being zero at the end point.
questions.answer: At the endpoint the solution contains the spectator ions $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ (a solution of potassium chloride), which are still able to conduct charge, so the conductivity is not zero.

questions.question:
The difference in the electronegativity of atoms can be used to determine the polarity of a bond. The electronegativity values for a range of elements are: hydrogen 2.1; carbon 2.5; nitrogen 3.0; oxygen 3.5; fluorine 4.0.

Using the information provided, compare the intramolecular bonds present in the molecules of separate pure samples of tetrafluoromethane and ammonia.
questions.answer:
| | Tetrafluoromethane | Ammonia |
|---|---|---|
| Formula | $\text{CF}_4$ | $\text{NH}_3$ |
| Electronegativity difference | $4.0-2.5=1.5$ | $3.0-2.1=0.9$ |
| Intramolecular bonds | Polar covalent (C–F) | Polar covalent (N–H) |

Both molecules contain polar covalent bonds between non-metal atoms, but the C–F bonds are more polar (larger electronegativity difference) than the N–H bonds.

questions.question: Explain the intermolecular forces present in pure samples of tetrafluoromethane ($\text{CF}_4$) and ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$).
questions.answer:
**$\text{CF}_4$:** the molecule is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so the dipoles of the four polar C–F bonds cancel and the molecule is non-polar. The only intermolecular forces between its molecules are dispersion forces.

**$\text{NH}_3$:** the molecule is pyramidal and the polar N–H bond dipoles do not cancel, so it is a polar molecule with a net dipole towards the more electronegative nitrogen. Hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen (which has a lone pair), so there is hydrogen bonding between the hydrogen of one molecule and the nitrogen of another, as well as dipole–dipole forces and dispersion forces.

questions.question:
The following scheme can be used to prepare an ester. Compound A is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$. Step 1 converts A to B, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. Step 2 converts B to C, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. Step 3 converts C to D, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. Step 4 reacts C and D to form E, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Identify compounds A, B, C, D and E.
questions.answer:
| Compound | Name |
|---|---|
| A | But-1-ene |
| B | 1-chlorobutane |
| C | Butan-1-ol |
| D | Butanoic acid |
| E | Butyl butanoate |

questions.question: For the scheme in part (a) (A $\xrightarrow{\text{Step 1}}$ B $\xrightarrow{\text{Step 2}}$ C $\xrightarrow{\text{Step 3}}$ D; C + D $\xrightarrow{\text{Step 4}}$ E), identify the reagents/conditions for steps 1, 2, 3 and 4 and the type of reaction in each step (e.g. oxidation).
questions.answer:
| Step | Reagents/conditions | Type of reaction |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $\text{HCl}$ | addition |
| 2 | Sodium hydroxide solution | substitution |
| 3 | Acidified potassium permanganate (or dichromate) solution, heated | oxidation |
| 4 | Concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst, heat under reflux (with C and D) | esterification (condensation) |

Note: the school's marking guide accepts adding HCl to but-1-ene as the route to 1-chlorobutane. In practice the addition of HCl to but-1-ene follows Markovnikov's rule and gives mainly 2-chlorobutane, so this step is not realistic, but it is the step the question intends.

questions.question: Outline two reasons for preparing an ester in the school laboratory under reflux.
questions.answer:
1. Heating under reflux allows the reaction mixture to be kept at a higher temperature (near its boiling point), which increases the reaction rate.
2. The condenser condenses the volatile reactants and products (alcohol, acid and ester) and returns them to the reaction flask, so none is lost by evaporation (and flammable vapours do not escape).

questions.question: The following model shows oil droplets in water with soap anions arranged around each droplet (the soap anion is drawn as a wavy non-polar tail with a circular polar head; the tails are in the oil and the heads face the water). Use the model to explain the formation of an emulsion.
questions.answer:
An emulsion is a mixture in which droplets of one liquid are dispersed in another liquid with which it is immiscible (here, oil droplets dispersed in water).

A soap anion (e.g. $\text{RCOO}^-$) has a long non-polar hydrocarbon tail and a polar (charged) carboxylate head. In the model the non-polar tails dissolve in the oil droplet through dispersion forces, while the polar carboxylate heads face outward and interact with the polar water molecules through ion–dipole forces and hydrogen bonding. This forms small spherical droplets (micelles) with the tails inside the oil and the heads on the surface. The negatively charged heads on the surfaces of different droplets repel each other, so the droplets do not coalesce and stay dispersed throughout the water, forming a stable emulsion.

questions.question: $20.0$ mL of $0.0010$ mol L$^{-1}$ barium chloride was mixed with $30.0$ mL of $0.20$ mol L$^{-1}$ sodium sulfate and the product was filtered. ($K_{sp}(\text{BaSO}_4)=1.08\times10^{-10}$.) Calculate the concentration of each ion in the filtrate.
questions.answer:
$\text{BaCl}_2(aq)+\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)\rightarrow\text{BaSO}_4(s)+2\text{NaCl}(aq)$

Concentrations after mixing (total volume 50.0 mL):
$[\text{Ba}^{2+}]=0.0010\times\frac{20}{50}=4.0\times10^{-4}$ M; $[\text{Cl}^-]=2\times4.0\times10^{-4}=8.0\times10^{-4}$ M
$[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]=0.20\times\frac{30}{50}=0.12$ M; $[\text{Na}^+]=2\times0.12=0.24$ M

$Q=[\text{Ba}^{2+}][\text{SO}_4^{2-}]=4.0\times10^{-4}\times0.12=4.8\times10^{-5}>K_{sp}$, so $\text{BaSO}_4$ precipitates.

Ba$^{2+}$ is the limiting ion, but some remains in solution at equilibrium: $\text{BaSO}_4(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)+\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)$. Sulfate is in large excess, so $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]\approx0.12$ M (the amount used, about $4\times10^{-4}$ M, is negligible). Then
$$[\text{Ba}^{2+}]=\frac{K_{sp}}{[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]}=\frac{1.08\times10^{-10}}{0.12}=9.0\times10^{-10}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}.$$
$\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ are spectator ions, so their concentrations are unchanged.

Filtrate: $[\text{Ba}^{2+}]=9\times10^{-10}$ M; $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]=0.12$ M; $[\text{Cl}^-]=8.0\times10^{-4}$ M; $[\text{Na}^+]=0.24$ M.

Note: the school's working has a slip, writing $Q=4.8\times10^{-10}$; the correct value is $4.8\times10^{-5}$. The conclusion is unchanged.

questions.question:
The student repeated the experiment with a different set of starting concentrations. The concentrations of the species in the filtrate were:

| Species | $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)$ | $\text{Cl}^-(aq)$ | $\text{Na}^+(aq)$ | $\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Concentration (mol L$^{-1}$) | $1.2\times10^{-7}$ | $1.6\times10^{-5}$ | $1.8\times10^{-3}$ | $8.9\times10^{-4}$ |

The filtrate was divided into two small beakers, labelled A and B. Beaker A had an equal volume of $0.10$ mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide added to it. Beaker B had an equal volume of $0.10$ mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{AgNO}_3$ added to it. Deduce whether a precipitate formed in either, or both, of the beakers. ($K_{sp}$: $\text{Ba(OH)}_2=2.55\times10^{-4}$; $\text{Ag}_2\text{SO}_4=1.2\times10^{-5}$; $\text{AgCl}=1.77\times10^{-10}$.)
questions.answer:
Adding an equal volume halves every concentration: $[\text{Ba}^{2+}]=6.0\times10^{-8}$, $[\text{Cl}^-]=8.0\times10^{-6}$, $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]=4.45\times10^{-4}$ M, and the added ions are $[\text{OH}^-]=0.050$ M (beaker A) or $[\text{Ag}^+]=0.050$ M (beaker B).

**Beaker A:** the only possible new precipitate is $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ ($\text{Na}^+$ salts are soluble, and $\text{BaSO}_4$ has already been filtered off and is only diluted). $\text{Ba(OH)}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)$:
$Q=[\text{Ba}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2=(6.0\times10^{-8})(0.050)^2=1.5\times10^{-10}<K_{sp}=2.55\times10^{-4}$, so **no precipitate** forms.

**Beaker B:** nitrates are soluble, so test $\text{Ag}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{AgCl}$.
$\text{Ag}_2\text{SO}_4$: $Q=[\text{Ag}^+]^2[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]=(0.050)^2(4.45\times10^{-4})=1.1\times10^{-6}<1.2\times10^{-5}$, so no $\text{Ag}_2\text{SO}_4$.
$\text{AgCl}$: $Q=[\text{Ag}^+][\text{Cl}^-]=(0.050)(8.0\times10^{-6})=4\times10^{-7}>1.77\times10^{-10}$, so a **precipitate of AgCl forms**.

Conclusion: no precipitate in beaker A; a precipitate (AgCl) forms in beaker B.

questions.question:
A chemist synthesises a series of molecules using the following reaction pathway: 1-bromopropane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$) $\xrightarrow{\text{Step 1}}$ propan-1-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) $\xrightarrow{\text{Step 2}}$ propene ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$).

Describe a relevant chemical test that could be used to confirm the identity of the functional group in the product of Step 1, with reference to the appropriate observation.
questions.answer: The product of Step 1 is an alcohol (propan-1-ol). A small piece of sodium metal could be added to a sample: vigorous bubbling of hydrogen gas is observed if an alcohol is present. (Alternatives: acidified potassium dichromate changes from orange to green on warming; acidified potassium permanganate changes from purple to colourless; ceric ammonium nitrate changes from yellow to red.)

questions.question: In the reaction pathway in part (a) (1-bromopropane $\rightarrow$ propan-1-ol $\rightarrow$ propene), describe a relevant chemical test that could be used to confirm the identity of the functional group in the product of Step 2, with reference to the appropriate observation.
questions.answer: The product of Step 2 is an alkene (propene). A few drops of bromine water (or acidified potassium permanganate solution) are added to a sample and shaken. If a C=C bond is present, the orange/brown bromine water is decolourised (or the purple permanganate becomes colourless).

questions.question:
Potash is a solid fertiliser supplement that can contain a variety of different potassium salts. A particular brand is known to advertise a claim that it contains only $\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4$, $\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3$ and $\text{KNO}_3$ in an optimised ratio by mass of $1:2:4$.

A $24.31$ g portion of fertiliser granules from this brand was completely dissolved in $0.500$ L of water. A $25.00$ mL aliquot of the solution was titrated with $0.100$ mol L$^{-1}$ barium nitrate according to the reactions
$$\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2(aq)+\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)\rightarrow\text{BaSO}_4(s)+2\text{KNO}_3(aq)$$
$$\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2(aq)+\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)\rightarrow\text{BaCO}_3(s)+2\text{KNO}_3(aq).$$
This precipitation titration was repeated three additional times and it was found that the average mass of dried precipitate obtained was $0.849$ g from an average titre volume of $40.90$ mL.

A separate $25.00$ mL aliquot of fertiliser solution was treated with $50$ mL of $0.197$ mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid. The resultant solution was then titrated with a standardised sodium hydroxide solution of concentration $0.179$ mol L$^{-1}$. This method was repeated multiple times to obtain the following results.

| Titre | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Volume of NaOH(aq) added (mL) | 24.10 | 22.35 | 22.45 | 22.40 |

Do the results from this experiment support the manufacturer's claim? Support your answer with calculations.
questions.answer:
**Back titration (carbonate).** Titre 1 is a rough/outlier and is disregarded: $V(\text{NaOH})=\frac{22.35+22.45+22.40}{3}=22.40$ mL.
$n(\text{NaOH})=0.179\times0.02240=4.01\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{HCl})_{\text{excess}}$.
$n(\text{HCl})_{\text{added}}=0.197\times0.050=9.85\times10^{-3}$ mol, so $n(\text{HCl})_{\text{reacted}}=9.85\times10^{-3}-4.01\times10^{-3}=5.84\times10^{-3}$ mol.
$\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3+2\text{HCl}\rightarrow2\text{KCl}+\text{H}_2\text{O}+\text{CO}_2$, so $n(\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3)_{\text{aliquot}}=2.92\times10^{-3}$ mol.
Scaling to the whole solution ($500/25=20$): $n=5.84\times10^{-2}$ mol, so $m(\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3)=5.84\times10^{-2}\times138.21=8.07$ g.

**Precipitation titration (sulfate).** $n(\text{BaCO}_3)=2.92\times10^{-3}$ mol, so $m(\text{BaCO}_3)=2.92\times10^{-3}\times197.3=0.576$ g.
$m(\text{BaSO}_4)=0.849-0.576=0.273$ g, so $n(\text{BaSO}_4)=\frac{0.273}{233.4}=1.17\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4)_{\text{aliquot}}$.
Whole solution: $n=20\times1.17\times10^{-3}=2.34\times10^{-2}$ mol, so $m(\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4)=2.34\times10^{-2}\times174.27=4.07$ g.
(Check: $n(\text{Ba}^{2+})=0.100\times0.04090=4.09\times10^{-3}$ mol $=2.92\times10^{-3}+1.17\times10^{-3}$.)

**Potassium nitrate by difference.** $m(\text{KNO}_3)=24.31-8.07-4.07=12.17$ g.

**Ratio.** $\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4:\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3:\text{KNO}_3=4.07:8.07:12.17\approx1:2:3$. This is not $1:2:4$, so the results do **not** support the manufacturer's claim.

Note: the school's working has a transposition slip ($2.43\times10^{-2}$ instead of $2.34\times10^{-2}$ mol), but the mass of 4.07 g it gives is the correct one.

questions.question:
The following data was obtained from the analysis of an organic compound with a molecular formula of $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$. The infrared spectrum shows a very strong absorption near $1750$ cm$^{-1}$ and C–H absorptions near 3000 and 2700 cm$^{-1}$ with no broad O–H absorption. The carbon-13 NMR spectrum has six signals, one at about 203 ppm and the others below 50 ppm. The proton NMR spectrum has signals at about 9.66 ppm (1H, triplet), 2.42 ppm (2H, doublet), 0.76 ppm (3H, triplet), 0.71 ppm (2H, quartet) and 0.90 ppm (6H, singlet).

Draw the structural formula of this compound that is consistent with all the information provided. Justify your selected structure with reference to the relevant features from each of the spectra.
questions.answer:
**Structure:** 3,3-dimethylpentanal, $\text{OHC-CH}_2\text{-C(CH}_3)_2\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

**Infrared:** the strong absorption at about 1750 cm$^{-1}$ shows a C=O bond. There is no broad O–H absorption at 2500–3300 cm$^{-1}$, so the compound is not an alcohol or carboxylic acid. With only one oxygen, the compound must be an aldehyde or ketone.

**Carbon-13 NMR:** there are 6 signals for 7 carbon atoms, so two carbons are in the same environment (two equivalent methyl groups). The signal at about 203 ppm is typical of the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde or ketone.

**Proton NMR:** the signal at 9.66 ppm (1H) is very far downfield, characteristic of an aldehyde $\text{-CHO}$ hydrogen (a ketone has none), and it is a triplet, so it is next to a $\text{CH}_2$. The 2.42 ppm signal (2H) is a doublet, so this $\text{CH}_2$ is next to one hydrogen (the CHO) and is therefore $\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ attached to a carbon with no hydrogens. The 3H triplet and 2H quartet (about 0.7–0.8 ppm) form an ethyl group, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, attached to a carbon with no hydrogens. The 6H singlet at 0.90 ppm is two equivalent methyl groups with no neighbouring hydrogens. The $\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, the ethyl group and the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups are therefore all joined to a quaternary carbon, giving the structure above (C: $1+1+1+2+2=7$; H: $1+2+6+5=14$).

questions.question:
A student is studying the oxidation of the manganate ion to the permanganate ion using a transition metal containing oxidant $\text{X}^{2+}$:
$$\text{MnO}_4^{2-}(aq)+\text{X}^{2+}(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{MnO}_4^-(aq)+\text{X}^+(aq)\qquad\Delta H=+77.7\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Calculate the mass of potassium manganate ($\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4$) required to make 25.0 mL of 0.0400 M solution.

The student (in the reaction $\text{MnO}_4^{2-}(aq)+\text{X}^{2+}(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{MnO}_4^-(aq)+\text{X}^+(aq)$, $\Delta H=+77.7$ kJ mol$^{-1}$) then adds 25.0 mL of the 0.0400 M manganate solution to 25.0 mL of 0.0600 M $\text{X}^{2+}$ solution in an insulated vessel containing a temperature sensor. The sensor reading is initially $24.1^\circ$C. Once equilibrium is established, the concentration of the manganate ion is 0.00800 M. Calculate the final temperature of the insulated vessel. (Assume the solution has the density and specific heat capacity of water, $4.184$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.)
questions.answer:
Initial $n(\text{MnO}_4^{2-})=0.0400\times0.0250=1.00\times10^{-3}$ mol. Total volume $=50.0$ mL, so final $n=0.00800\times0.0500=4.0\times10^{-4}$ mol.
Moles reacted $=1.00\times10^{-3}-4.0\times10^{-4}=6.0\times10^{-4}$ mol.
The reaction is endothermic, so the solution absorbs heat: $q=6.0\times10^{-4}\times77.7\times1000=46.6$ J (taken from the solution).
$m(\text{solution})\approx50$ g, so $\Delta T=\dfrac{q}{mc}=\dfrac{46.6}{50\times4.184}=0.22^\circ$C (a decrease).
Final temperature $=24.1-0.22=23.9^\circ$C.

questions.question: For the equilibrium in part (b) (25.0 mL of 0.0400 M $\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$ mixed with 25.0 mL of 0.0600 M $\text{X}^{2+}$, with $[\text{MnO}_4^{2-}]=0.00800$ M at equilibrium), justify the value $K_{eq}=1$ for this reaction.
For the equilibrium in part (b) ($\Delta H=+77.7$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, $K_{eq}=1$ at about $24^\circ$C), explain what can be deduced about $\Delta G$ and $\Delta S$ for this reaction.
questions.answer:
$K_{eq}=1$ at about $24^\circ$C means that neither reactants nor products are favoured at equilibrium, which corresponds to $\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K=0$.

Since $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$ and $\Delta H$ is large and positive ($+77.7$ kJ mol$^{-1}$), $\Delta G=0$ is only possible if $T\Delta S$ is also positive and equal in size to $\Delta H$. Hence $\Delta S$ must be positive: $\Delta S=\dfrac{\Delta H}{T}=\dfrac{77\,700}{297}\approx260$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$.
